where the columns of **U** ∈ ℝ^(*n* × *n*) are the eigenvectors of **A** and **Λ** is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues of **A**, i.e.,

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1201.jpg)

If the eigenvectors of **A** are linearly independent, then the matrix **U** will be invertible, so

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1202.jpg)

A matrix that can be written in this form is called **diagonalizable**.

### 7.4.3 Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetric matrices

When **A** is real and symmetric, it can be shown that all the eigenvalues are real, and the eigenvectors are **orthonormal**, i.e., ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1203.jpg) if *i* ≠ *j*, and ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1204.jpg), where ***u***_(*i*) are the eigenvectors. In matrix form, this becomes **U**^(T)**U** = **UU**^(T) = **I**; hence we see that **U** is an orthogonal matrix.

We can therefore represent **A** as

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1205.jpg)

Thus multiplying by any symmetric matrix **A** can be interpreted as multiplying by a rotation matrix **U**^(T), a scaling matrix **Λ**, followed by an inverse rotation **U**.

Once we have diagonalized a matrix, it is easy to invert. Since **A** = **UΛU**^(T), where **U**^(T) = **U**⁻¹, we have

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1206.jpg)

This corresponds to rotating, unscaling, and then rotating back.

**7.4.3.1 Checking for positive definiteness**

We can also use the diagonalization property to show that a symmetric matrix is positive definite iff all its eigenvalues are positive. To see this, note that

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1207.jpg)

where ***y*** = **U**^(T)***x***. Because ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1208.jpg) is always nonnegative, the sign of this expression depends entirely on the *λ_(i)*’s. If all *λ_(i)* \> 0, then the matrix is positive definite; if all *λ_(i)* ≥ 0, it is positive semidefinite. Likewise, if all *λ_(i)* \< 0 or *λ_(i)* ≤ 0, then **A** is negative definite or negative semidefinite respectively. Finally, if **A** has both positive and negative eigenvalues, it is indefinite.

### 7.4.5 Standardizing and whitening data

Suppose we have a dataset **X** ∈ ℝ^(*N* × *D*). It is common to preprocess the data so that each column has zero mean and unit variance. This is called the **PCA whitening** matrix. (We discuss PCA in [Section 20.1](#chapter020.xhtml#Sec_20.1).) Let ***y* = W**_(*pca*)***x*** be a transformed vector. We can check that its covariance is white as follows:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1216.jpg)

The whitening matrix is not unique, since any rotation of it, **W** = **RW**_(*pca*), will still maintain the whitening property, i.e., **W**^(T)**W** = **Σ**⁻¹. For example, if we take **R** = **E**, we get

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1217.jpg)

This is called **Mahalanobis whitening** or **ZCA**. (ZCA stands for “zero-phase component analysis”, and was introduced in \[BS97\].) The advantage of ZCA whitening over PCA whitening is that the resulting transformed data is as close as possible to the original data (in the least squares sense) \[Amo17\]. This is illustrated in [Figure 7.7](#chapter007.xhtml#Fig_7-7). When applied to images, the ZCA transformed data vectors still look like images. This is useful when the method is used inside a deep learning system \[KH09\].

### 7.4.6 Power method

We now describe a simple iterative method for computing the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue of a real, symmetric matrix; this is called the **power method**. This can be useful when the matrix is very large but sparse. For example, it used by Google’s **PageRank** to compute the stationary distribution of the transition matrix of the world wide web (a matrix of size about 3 billion by 3 billion!). In [Section 7.4.7](#chapter007.xhtml#Sec_7.4.7), we will see how to use this method to compute subsequent eigenvectors and values.

Let **A** be a matrix with orthonormal eigenvectors ***u***_(*i*) and eigenvalues *\|λ*₁*\| \> \|λ*₂*\| ≥ ⋯ ≥ \|λ_(m)\| ≥* 0, so **A** = **UΛU**^(T). Let ***v***₍₀₎ be an arbitrary vector in the range of **A**, so **A*x*** = ***v***₍₀₎ for some ***x***. Hence we can write ***v***₍₀₎ as

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1218.jpg)

for some constants *a_(i)*. We can now repeatedly multiply ***v*** by **A** and renormalize:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1219.jpg)

(We normalize at each iteration for numerical stability.)

Since ***v**_(t)* is a multiple of **A**^(*t*)***v***₀, we have

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1220.jpg)

since ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1221.jpg) for *k* \> 1 (assuming the eigenvalues are sorted in descending order). So we see that this converges to ***u***₁, although not very quickly (the error is reduced by approximately \|*λ*₂/*λ*₁\| at each iteration). The only requirement is that the initial guess satisfy ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1222.jpg), which will be true for a random ***v***₀ with high probability.

We now discuss how to compute the corresponding eigenvalue, *λ*₁. Define the **Rayleigh quotient** to be

Hence

Thus we can easily compute *λ*₁ from ***u***₁ and **A**. See code.probml.ai/book1/power_method_demo for a demo.

### 7.4.7 Deflation

Suppose we have computed the first eigenvector and value ***u***₁, *λ*₁ by the power method. We now describe how to compute subsequent eigenvectors and values. Since the eigenvectors are orthonormal, and the eigenvalues are real, we can project out the ***u***₁ component from the matrix as follows:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1225.jpg)

This is called matrix **deflation**. We can then apply the power method to **A**⁽²⁾, which will find the largest eigenvector/value in the subspace orthogonal to ***u***₁.

In [Section 20.1.2](#chapter020.xhtml#Sec_20.1.2), we show that the optimal estimate Ŵ for the PCA model (described in [Section 20.1](#chapter020.xhtml#Sec_20.1)) is given by the first *K* eigenvectors of the empirical covariance matrix. Hence deflation can be used to implement PCA. It can also be modified to implement sparse PCA \[Mac09\].

### 7.4.8 Eigenvectors optimize quadratic forms

We can use matrix calculus to solve an optimization problem in a way that leads directly to eigenvalue/eigenvector analysis. Consider the following, equality constrained optimization problem:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1226.jpg)

for a symmetric matrix **A** ∈ S^(*n*). A standard way of solving optimization problems with equality constraints is by forming the Lagrangian, an objective function that includes the equality constraints (see [Section 8.5.1](#chapter008.xhtml#Sec_8.5.1)). The Lagrangian in this case can be given by

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1227.jpg)

where *λ* is called the Lagrange multiplier associated with the equality constraint. It can be established that for *x*\* to be a optimal point to the problem, the gradient of the Lagrangian has to be zero at *x*\* (this is not the only condition, but it is required). That is,

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1228.jpg)

Notice that this is just the linear equation **A*x*** = ***λx***. This shows that the only points which can possibly maximize (or minimize) ***x***^(T)**A*x*** assuming ***x***^(T)***x*** = 1 are the eigenvectors of **A**.

## 7.5 Singular value decomposition (SVD)

We now discuss the SVD, which generalizes EVD to rectangular matrices.

### 7.5.1 Basics

Any (real) *m × n* matrix **A** can be decomposed as

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1229.jpg)

where **U** is an *m × m* whose columns are orthornormal (so **U**^(T)**U** = **I**_(*m*)), **V** is *n × n* matrix whose rows and columns are orthonormal (so **V**^(T)**V** = **VV**^(T) = **I**_(*n*)), and **S** is a *m* × *n* matrix containing the *r* = min(*m, n*) **singular values** *σ_(i)* ≥ 0 on the main diagonal, with 0s filling the rest of the matrix. The columns of **U** are the left **singular vectors**, and the columns of **V** are the right singular vectors. This is called the **singular value decomposition** or **SVD** of the matrix. See [Figure 7.8](#chapter007.xhtml#Fig_7-8) for an example.

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1230.jpg)

*Figure 7.8: SVD decomposition of a matrix,* **A** = **USV^(T)**. *The shaded parts of each matrix are not computed in the economy-sized version. (a) Tall skinny matrix. (b) Short wide matrix.*

As is apparent from [Figure 7.8a](#chapter007.xhtml#Fig_7-8), if *m* \> *n*, there are at most *n* singular values, so the last *m* − *n* columns of **U** are irrelevant (since they will be multiplied by 0). The **economy sized SVD**, also called a **thin SVD**, avoids computing these unnecessary elements. In other words, if we write the **U** matrix as **U** = \[**U**₁, **U**₂\], we only compute **U**₁. [Figure 7.8b](#chapter007.xhtml#Fig_7-8) shows the opposite case, where *m* \< *n*, where we represent **V** = \[**V**₁; **V**₂\], and only compute **V**₁.

The cost of computing the SVD is *O*(min(*mn*², *m*²*n*)). Details on how it works can be found in standard linear algebra textbooks.

### 7.5.2 Connection between SVD and EVD

If **A** is real, symmetric and positive definite, then the singular values are equal to the eigenvalues, and the left and right singular vectors are equal to the eigenvectors (up to a sign change):

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1231.jpg)

Note, however, that NumPy always returns the singular values in decreasing order, whereas the eigenvalues need not necessarily be sorted.

In general, for an arbitrary real matrix **A**, if **A** = **USV**^(T), we have

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1232.jpg)

Hence

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1233.jpg)

so the eigenvectors of **A**^(T)**A** are equal to **V**, the right singular vectors of **A**, and the eigenvalues of **A**^(T)**A** are equal to **D**_(*n*) = **S**^(T)**S**, which is an *n* × *n* diagonal matrix containing the squared singular values. Similarly

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1234.jpg)

so the eigenvectors of **AA**^(T) are equal to **U**, the left singular vectors of **A**, and the eigenvalues of **AA**^(T) are equal to **D**_(*m*) = **SS**^(T), which is an *m × m* diagonal matrix containing the squared singular values. In summary,

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1235.jpg)

If we just use the computed (non-zero) parts in the economy-sized SVD, then we can define

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1236.jpg)

Note also that an EVD does not always exist, even for square **A**, whereas an SVD always exists.

Let **A** = **USV^(*T*)** be the SVD of **A**, and let ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1254.jpg), where we use the first *K* columns of **U** and **V**. This can be shown to be the optimal rank *K* approximation, in the sense that it minimizes ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1255.jpg).

If *K* = *r* = rank(**A**), there is no error introduced by this decomposition. But if *K* \< *r*, we incur some error. This is called a **truncated SVD**. If the singular values die off quickly, as is typical in natural data (see e.g., [Figure 7.10](#chapter007.xhtml#Fig_7-10)), the error will be small. The total number of parameters needed to represent an *N* × *D* matrix using a rank *K* approximation is

One can show that the error in this approximation is given by

where *σ_(k)* is the *k*’th singular value of **A**. Furthermore, one can show that the SVD offers the best rank *K* approximation to a matrix (best in the sense of minimizing the above Frobenius norm).

## 7.6 Other matrix decompositions \*

In this section, we briefly review some other useful matrix decompositions.

### 7.6.1 LU factorization

We can factorize any square matrix **A** into a product of a lower triangular matrix **L** and an upper triangular matrix **U**. For example,

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1258.jpg)

In general we may need to permute the entries in the matrix before creating this decomposition. To see this, suppose *a*₁₁ = 0. Since *a*₁₁ = *l*₁₁*u*₁₁, this means either *l*₁₁ or *u*₁₁ or both must be zero, but that would imply **L** or **U** are singular. To avoid this, the first step of the algorithm can simply reorder the rows so that the first element is nonzero. This is repeated for subsequent steps. We can denote this process by

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1259.jpg)

where **P** is a permutation matrix, i.e., a square binary matrix where *P_(ij)* = 1 if row *j* gets permuted to row *i*. This is called **partial pivoting**.

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1260.jpg)

*Figure 7.11: Illustration of QR decomposition,* **A** = **QR**, *where* **Q**^(T)**Q** = **I** *and* **R** *is upper triangular. (a) Tall, skinny matrix. The shaded parts are not computed in the economy-sized version, since they are not needed. (b) Short, wide matrix.*

### 7.6.2 QR decomposition

Suppose we have **A** ∈ ℝ^(*m* × *n*) representing a set of linearly independent basis vectors (so *m* ≥ *n*), and we want to find a series of orthonormal vectors ***q***₁, ***q***₂, … that span the successive subspaces of span(***a***₁), span(***a***₁, ***a***₂), etc. In other words, we want to find vectors ***q***_(*j*) and coefficients *r_(ij)* such that

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1261.jpg)

We can write this

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1262.jpg)

so we see ***q***₁ spans the space of ***a***₁, and ***q***₁ and ***q***₂ span the space of {***a***₁, ***a***₂}, etc.

In matrix notation, we have

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1263.jpg)

where ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Qcap.jpg) is *m* × *n* with orthonormal columns and ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Rcap.jpg) is *n* × *n* and upper triangular. This is called a **reduced QR** or **economy sized QR** factorization of **A**; see [Figure 7.11](#chapter007.xhtml#Fig_7-11).

A full QR factorization appends an additional *m* − *n* orthonormal columns to ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Qcap.jpg) so it becomes a square, orthogonal matrix **Q**, which satisfies **QQ**^(T) = **Q**^(T)**Q** = **I**. Also, we append rows made of zero to ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Rcap.jpg) so it becomes an *m* × *n* matrix that is still upper triangular, called **R**: see [Figure 7.11](#chapter007.xhtml#Fig_7-11). The zero entries in **R** “kill off” the new columns in **Q**, so the result is the same as ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1264.jpg) .

QR decomposition is commonly used to solve systems of linear equations, as we discuss in [Section 11.2.2.3](#chapter011.xhtml#Sec_11.2.2.3).

### 7.6.3 Cholesky decomposition

Any symmetric positive definite matrix can be factorized as **A** = **R**^(T)**R**, where **R** is upper triangular with real, positive diagonal elements. (This can also be written as **A** = **LL**^(T), where **L** = **R**^(T) is lower triangular.) This is called a **Cholesky factorization** or **matrix square root**. In NumPy, this is implemented by np.linalg.cholesky. The computational complexity of this operation is *O*(*V* ³), where *V* is the number of variables, but can be less for sparse matrices. Below we give some applications of this factorization.

**7.6.3.1 Application: Sampling from an MVN**

The Cholesky decomposition of a covariance matrix can be used to sample from a multivariate Gaussian. Let ***y*** ~ N (***μ,* Σ**) and **Σ** = **LL**^(T). We first sample ***x*** ~ N (**0, I**), which is easy because it just requires sampling from *d* separate 1d Gaussians. We then set ***y*** = **L*x*** + ***μ***. This is valid since

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1265.jpg)

See code.probml.ai/book1/cholesky_demo for some code.

## 7.7 Solving systems of linear equations \*

An important application of linear algebra is the study of systems of linear equations. For example, consider the following set of 3 equations:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1266.jpg)

We can represent this in matrix-vector form as follows:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1267.jpg)

where

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1268.jpg)

The solution is ***x*** = \[1, −2, −2\].

In general, if we have *m* equations and *n* unknowns, then **A** will be a *m* × *n* matrix, and ***b*** will be a *m* × 1 vector. If *m* = *n* (and **A** is full rank), there is a single unique solution. If *m* \< *n*, the system is **underdetermined**, so there is not a unique solution. If *m* \> *n*, the system is **overdetermined**, since there are more constraints than unknowns, and not all the lines intersect at the same point. See [Figure 7.12](#chapter007.xhtml#Fig_7-12) for an illustration. We discuss how to compute solutions in each of these cases below.

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1269.jpg)

*Figure 7.12: Solution of a set of m linear equations in n* = 2 *variables. (a) m* = 1 *\< n so the system is underdetermined. We show the minimal norm solution as a blue circle. (The dotted red line is orthogonal to the line, and its length is the distance to the origin.) (b) m* = *n* = 2, *so there is a unique solution. (c) m* = 3 *\> n, so there is no unique solution. We show the least squares solution.*

### 7.7.1 Solving square systems

In the case where *m* = *n*, we can solve for ***x*** by computing an LU decomposition, **A** = **LU**, and then proceeding as follows:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1270.jpg)

The crucial point is that **L** and **U** are both triangular matrices, so we can avoid taking matrix inverses, and use a method known as **backsubstitution** instead.

In particular, we can solve ***y*** = **L⁻¹*b*** without taking inverses as follows. First we write

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1271.jpg)

We start by solving *L*₁₁*y*₁ = *b*₁ to find *y*₁ and then substitute this in to solve

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1272.jpg)

for *y*₂. We repeat this recursively. This process is often denoted by the **backslash operator, *y*** = **L** \\ ***b***. Once we have ***y***, we can solve ***x*** = **U**⁻¹***y*** using backsubstitution in a similar manner.

The corresponding solution ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1291.jpg) is the **ordinary least squares** (**OLS**) solution, which is given by

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1293.jpg)

If **A** is full rank (so the columns of **A** are linearly independent), then **H** is positive definite, since for any ***v*** \> **0**, we have

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1294.jpg)

Hence in the full rank case, the least squares objective has a unique global minimum.

## 7.8 Matrix calculus

The topic of **calculus** concerns computing “rates of change” of functions as we vary their inputs. It is of vital importance to machine learning, as well as almost every other numerical discipline. In this section, we review some standard results. In some cases, we use some concepts and notation from matrix algebra, which we cover in [Chapter 7](#chapter007.xhtml). For more details on these results from a deep learning perspective, see \[PH18\].

### 7.8.1 Derivatives

Consider a scalar-argument function *f* : ℝ → ℝ. We define its **derivative** at a point *a* to be the quantity

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1295.jpg)

assuming the limit exists. This measures how quickly the output changes when we move a small distance in input space away from *x* (i.e., the “rate of change” of the function). We can interpret *f*′(*x*) as the slope of the tangent line at *f*(*x*), and hence

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1296.jpg)

for small *h*.

We can compute a **finite difference** approximation to the derivative by using a finite step size *h*, as follows:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1297.jpg)

The smaller the step size *h*, the better the estimate, although if *h* is too small, there can be errors due to numerical cancellation.

We can think of differentiation as an operator that maps functions to functions, *D*(*f*) = *f*′, where *f*′(*x*) computes the derivative at *x* (assuming the derivative exists at that point). The use of the prime symbol *f*′ to denote the derivative is called **Lagrange notation**. The second derivative function, which measures how quickly the gradient is changing, is denoted by *f*″. The *n*’th derivative function is denoted *f*^((*n*)).

Alternatively, we can use **Leibniz notation**, in which we denote the function by *y* = *f*(*x*), and its derivative by ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1298.jpg) or ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1299.jpg) . To denote the evaluation of the derivative at a point *a*, we write ![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1300.jpg) .

### 7.8.2 Gradients

We can extend the notion of derivatives to handle vector-argument functions, *f* : ℝ^(*n*) → ℝ, by defining the **partial derivative** of *f* with respect to *x_(i)* to be

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1301.jpg)

where ***e***_(*i*) is the *i*’th unit vector.

The **gradient** of a function at a point ***x*** is the vector of its partial derivatives:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1302.jpg)

To emphasize the point at which the gradient is evaluated, we can write

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1303.jpg)

We see that the operator **∇** (pronounced “nabla”) maps a function *f* : ℝ^(*n*) → ℝ to another function ***g*** : ℝ^(*n*) → ℝ^(*n*). Since ***g***() is a vector-valued function, it is known as a **vector field**. By contrast, the derivative function *f*′ is a **scalar field**.

### 7.8.3 Directional derivative

The **directional derivative** measures how much the function *f* : ℝ^(*n*) → ℝ changes along a direction ***v*** in space. It is defined as follows

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1304.jpg)

We can approximate this numerically using 2 function calls to *f*, regardless of *n*. By contrast, a numerical approximation to the standard gradient vector takes *n* + 1 calls (or 2*n* if using central differences).

Note that the directional derivative along ***v*** is the scalar product of the gradient ***g*** and the vector ***v***:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1305.jpg)

### 7.8.4 Total derivative \*

Suppose that some of the arguments to the function depend on each other. Concretely, suppose the function has the form *f*(*t, x*(*t*), *y*(*t*)). We define the **total derivative** of *f* wrt *t* as follows:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1306.jpg)

If we multiply both sides by the differential *dt*, we get the **total differential**

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1307.jpg)

This measures how much *f* changes when we change *t*, both via the direct effect of *t* on *f*, but also indirectly, via the effects of *t* on *x* and *y*.

### 7.8.5 Jacobian

Consider a function that maps a vector to another vector, ***f*** : ℝ^(*n*) → ℝ^(*m*). The **Jacobian matrix** of this function is an *m* × *n* matrix of partial derivatives:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1308.jpg)

Note that we lay out the results in the same orientation as the output ***f***; this is sometimes called numerator layout or the Jacobian formulation.^([4](#chapter007.xhtml#footnote_32))

**7.8.5.1 Multiplying Jacobians and vectors**

The **Jacobian vector product** or **JVP** is defined to be the operation that corresponds to right-multiplying the Jacobian matrix **J** ∈ ℝ^(*m* × *n*) by a vector ***v*** ∈ ℝ^(*n*):

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1309.jpg)

So we can see that we can approximate this numerically using just 2 calls to ***f***.

The **vector Jacobian product** or **VJP** is defined to be the operation that corresponds to left-multiplying the Jacobian matrix **J** ∈ ℝ^(*m*×*n*) by a vector ***u*** ∈ ℝ^(*m*):

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1310.jpg)

The JVP is more efficient if *m* ≥ *n*, and the VJP is more efficient if *m* ≤ *n*. See [Section 13.3](#chapter013.xhtml#Sec_13.3) for details on how this can be used to perform automatic differentiation in a computation graph such as a DNN.

**7.8.5.2 Jacobian of a composition**

Sometimes it is useful to take the Jacobian of the composition of two functions. Let *h*(***x***) = *g*(*f*(***x***)). By the chain rule of calculus, we have

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1311.jpg)

For example, suppose *f* : ℝ → ℝ² and *g* : ℝ² → ℝ². We have

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1312.jpg)

### 7.8.6 Hessian

For a function *f* : ℝ^(*n*) → ℝ that is twice differentiable, we define the **Hessian matrix** as the (symmetric) *n* × *n* matrix of second partial derivatives:

![art](markdown/Probabilistic Machine Learning _ An Introduction/media/images/Art_P1313.jpg)

We see that the Hessian is the Jacobian of the gradient.
